newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel delays hearings for CIA nominee.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel delays hearings for CIA nominee.

text.p: The Senate Intelligence Committee on Thursday delayed hearings on President Bill Clinton's nominee to head the CIA, deciding to await a Justice Department investigation into Anthony Lake's stock dealings.
The panel's Republican chairman, Richard Shelby of Alabama, said it would be "premature and short-sighted" for the committee to preempt the inquiry.

The Justice Department's Public Integrity Section has been looking into possible conflict of interest questions because Lake failed to take timely action on orders to sell his personal holdings in energy stocks when he was appointed White House National Security Adviser in 1993.

House Republicans also have asked for an investigation of whether Lake and other U.S. officials lied to Congress about the Clinton administration's position on Iran's 1994 arming of Bosnian forces. But the Justice Department declined to say if Attorney General Janet Reno had agreed to the request.

"I believe it would be premature and short-sighted for this committee to preempt the Justice Department's criminal investigation into Mr. Lake's handling of his investments, as well as allegations that Mr. Lake lied to Congress," Shelby said in a written statement.
Lake's confirmation hearings, planned for Feb. 11, had been tentatively rescheduled for the week of Feb. 25 pending the status of the Justice Department investigation, Shelby said.
Senate critics have warned they will challenge Lake's handling of the Iran-Bosnia policy, which the nominee subsequently acknowledged had been a mistake.
But Clinton has stood firmly behind Lake and the White House on Thursday sought to play down the postponement of his confirmation hearings.
"It's a delay from one end of the (Congressional) recess to the other. This will give Mr. Lake more time to prove his qualifications and integrity to the committee," spokesman David Johnson said.

"We of course want to work with the committee to clear up any issues that they have outstanding. And it goes without saying that the president continues to believe that Mr. Lake will serve as a very strong and well-qualified director of Central Intelligence," he said.
